new.title: Stand still at Kazerne Dossin in Mechelen
new.desc: From this former barracks in Mechelen, more than 25,000 Jews and Roma were deported to Auschwitz-Birkenau between 1942 and 1944. Today it is a memorial, museum and research centre on the Holocaust and human rights.
new.tip: Start at the memorial in the old barracks courtyard, then cross to the museum; the top floor looks out over Mechelen's rooftops.

new.title: Lose yourself in the Begijnhof of Lier
new.desc: Around 160 little houses on eleven narrow lanes make Lier's beguinage one of the best preserved in Flanders and part of the UNESCO-listed group of Flemish beguinages. The last beguine only left in 1984.
new.tip: Enter through the Baroque gate from 1690 and walk quietly: people still live here. Combine it with the Zimmertoren a few minutes away.

new.title: See Leonardo's Last Supper in Tongerlo Abbey
new.desc: In a quiet Norbertine abbey near Westerlo hangs a huge 16th-century copy of Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper, bought by the abbot in 1545. Experts call it the most faithful copy there is, and some think the master himself painted a few of the heads.
new.tip: The painting has its own Da Vinci Museum inside the abbey grounds; walk the lime-tree lane and the abbey park afterwards.

new.title: Find the Baroque chapel in Turnhout's Begijnhof
new.desc: Turnhout's UNESCO-listed beguinage, probably founded in the 13th century, wraps around a green courtyard with a Baroque church from the 1660s. It sits right next to the moated castle of the Dukes of Brabant.
new.tip: Turnhout is the world capital of playing cards: pair the beguinage with the Nationaal Museum van de Speelkaart in an old card factory, which has a combi ticket.

new.title: Hear the story of Saint Dimpna in Geel
new.desc: The Sint-Dimpnakerk holds the shrine of an Irish princess who became the patron saint of mental illness. Her cult gave rise to Geel's unique tradition, more than seven centuries old, of local families taking in psychiatric 'boarders' as part of the household.
new.tip: Look for the carved altarpiece telling Dimpna's legend, then cross the street to the Gasthuismuseum, the old pilgrims' hospital with its chapel and cloister.

new.title: Spin Mercator's globes in Sint-Niklaas
new.desc: Gerardus Mercator was born just down the road in Rupelmonde, and the renovated MAP-Mercator museum shows more than 100 globes, original Mercator globes among them, plus what is called the world's largest atlas.
new.tip: Try the interactive station that projects your own face onto different map projections, then walk to the Grote Markt, the largest market square in Belgium.

new.title: Walk under the cherry trees of Hasselt's Japanese Garden
new.desc: A garden built with Hasselt's Japanese twin town Itami, with a ceremonial tea house, waterfalls, stone lanterns and koi ponds. In April the cherry blossom turns it pink and the Itami Festival celebrates the season.
new.tip: Come early in the blossom weeks to beat the crowds; in autumn the Kikumatsuri chrysanthemum festival is the quieter alternative.

new.title: Go under the basilica in Tongeren
new.desc: Tongeren is the oldest town in Belgium, and beneath its Onze-Lieve-Vrouwebasiliek lie the traces of Roman houses and a medieval town centre. The Teseum next door shows them along with a treasury of reliquaries and choir books.
new.tip: Book the underground archaeological visit; the Gallo-Romeins Museum is a short walk away if you want the full Roman story.

new.title: Step into Belgium's oldest pharmacy in Maaseik
new.desc: On the lime-shaded Markt of Maaseik, where a statue honours the Van Eyck brothers who were probably born here, an apothecary shop stayed open from 1704 to 1959. Its jars, scales and herb garden are now a museum.
new.tip: Buy a combi ticket at the tourist office on the Markt: it also covers the archaeology and bakery museums in the same Museactron complex.

new.title: Look out over the Mechelse Heide in the national park
new.desc: Hoge Kempen is Flanders' only national park, and the Mechelse Heide near Maasmechelen is its classic picture: rolling purple heath, sandy paths and pine woods on the edge of the Kempen plateau.
new.tip: Start at the Mechelse Heide entrance gate; late August is when the heather is at its most purple.

new.title: Order a Mechelse koekoek in Mechelen
new.desc: The 'Mechelen cuckoo' is not a bird you hear but a big black-and-white chicken bred around Mechelen since the 1850s. Almost lost after the war, the slow-growing breed is back on farms and menus, prized for its darker, tastier meat.
new.tip: Look for 'Mechelse koekoek' on the menus of the brasseries around the Grote Markt; it is often served simply roasted or with a creamy sauce.

new.title: Drink a Tripel at Café Trappisten in Westmalle
new.desc: The monks of Westmalle Abbey, who invented the tripel style in the 1930s, own exactly one café: Café Trappisten, across the road from the abbey. With luck you can also try the light Westmalle Extra, brewed mainly for the monks themselves.
new.tip: The abbey and brewery are closed to visitors, but a walking loop around the abbey grounds starts at the café. Buses from Antwerpen stop at Westmalle Abdij.

new.title: Taste jenever where it is distilled in Hasselt
new.desc: Hasselt jenever is a protected regional name, and the Nationaal Jenevermuseum occupies a 17th-century monastery farm that worked as a distillery for almost two centuries. The 19th-century steam distillery still produces grain jenevers.
new.tip: End the visit with a tasting; in October the whole city celebrates the spirit at the Jeneverfeesten.

new.title: Dunk Hasselt speculaas in a Hasseltse koffie
new.desc: In Hasselt it is called speculaas, not speculoos, and it is thicker and softer than the usual biscuit. Locals pair it with Hasseltse koffie, a strong mix of coffee extract and local jenever.
new.tip: Bakers Cools and Bakkersdochter are known for their speculaas; Chocoladehuis Boon sells a praline with speculaas and juniper you only find in Hasselt.

new.title: Crunch a knapkoek in Maaseik
new.desc: Maaseik's own sweet, crisp biscuit has been baked in town since 1648. The Maasland around it also makes the Eyckedröpke beer, named after the town's famous painters.
new.tip: Visit on a Wednesday morning, when the weekly market fills the Markt, and pick up knapkoeken at a local bakery.

new.title: Spread Loonse stroop in Borgloon
new.desc: Borgloon, in the heart of the Haspengouw orchards, is known for its fruit syrup cooked from apples and pears. The town even opens the blossom season with the Loonse Stroopfeesten.
new.tip: Buy a pot in Borgloon and eat it the local way, on a slice of bread or with cheese; combine it with a blossom ride in April.

new.title: Sip Maasvallei wine at Aldeneyck
new.desc: Belgium makes wine, and some of the best known comes from the Aldeneyck estate on the banks of the Maas near Maaseik. The Maasvallei's mild gravelly slopes suit white grapes surprisingly well.
new.tip: Cycle there from Maaseik along the Maas and stop in the riverside village of Aldeneik with its old church.

new.title: Walk the floating Dijlepad in Mechelen
new.desc: The river Dijle is half hidden between Mechelen's old houses, but a wooden walkway now lets you follow it at water level past overgrown gardens and waterfront facades that were once only visible by boat.
new.tip: Go after dark, when thousands of small spotlights light up the path; start at the Zoutwerf and stop at the little terrace of café De Gouden Vis on the water.

new.title: Cycle through the water at Bokrijk
new.desc: Near Genk, a sunken cycle path cuts straight through a pond in the De Wijers wetlands: about 200 metres with the water at eye level on both sides and ducks paddling past your head.
new.tip: Follow cycle junctions 98 to 91 on the Limburg network; it is free and open all year, and Bokrijk station is the easiest start by train.
new.q: Fietsen door het water Bokrijk Genk

new.title: Ride up into the treetops in Hechtel-Eksel
new.desc: In the Pijnven pine forest of Bosland, a gently sloping cycle path climbs in two big loops up to ten metres high, so you pedal among the crowns of the trees.
new.tip: Head for cycle junction 272; walkers can use it too, and it pairs well with a day of cycling through the water at Bokrijk.
new.q: Fietsen door de bomen Pijnven Hechtel-Eksel

new.title: Step back in time at Bokrijk open-air museum
new.desc: Farmhouses, mills, chapels and whole village streets from all over Flanders were moved to the woods of Bokrijk near Genk, where costumed actors and craftspeople bring old rural life back to life.
new.tip: Plan a full day and add the arboretum and the cycle-through-the-water path in the same domain; check the season dates before you go.

new.title: Go deep down and high up at C-mine in Genk
new.desc: The old Winterslag coal mine in Genk is now a design and culture hub. The C-mine expedition takes you through the mine's underground passages and up to the top of the headframe.
new.tip: Afterwards, get lost in the steel Labyrinth on the square and look in on the studio of ceramist Pieter Stockmans in a former warehouse.

new.title: Hunt for treasures at Tongeren's Sunday antiques market
new.desc: Every Sunday, around 350 stallholders and dozens of antique dealers fill the streets around the Veemarkt in Tongeren for what is often called the biggest antiques market in the Benelux.
new.tip: Arrive early, the best finds go first; part of the market is under cover in the Julianus car park, so it works in the rain too.

new.title: Cycle through the Haspengouw blossom
new.desc: In spring the orchards between Sint-Truiden and Borgloon turn white and pink with apple, pear and cherry blossom over gently rolling hills, in Belgium's biggest fruit region.
new.tip: Rent a bike at the fietspunt at Sint-Truiden station and follow the numbered junctions towards Borgloon; check Sint-Truiden's bloesemmeter to time your trip.

new.title: Watch the balloons rise at the Vredefeesten in Sint-Niklaas
new.desc: On the first weekend of September, Sint-Niklaas celebrates its 1944 liberation and dozens of hot-air balloons take off from the Grote Markt, the largest market square in Belgium.
new.tip: Balloons launch in the early evening when the wind allows; stay on Saturday for the fireworks.
